ai.title: Broad Ligament Varices
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Broad ligament varices are dilated venous channels in the broad ligament, often linked to portal hypertension or pelvic congestion. They present as small bluish‑red lesions on laparoscopy and may cause chronic pelvic pain or bleeding.

b: Diagnosed by direct visualisation (laparoscopy, laparotomy)
Ultrasound with Doppler can show tubular, compressible, low‑resistance flow in the ligament
sections.p: Broad ligament varices are abnormal dilatations of veins within the broad ligament, visible as 0.2–0.4 cm bluish‑red raised lesions on laparoscopy or during surgery.

b: Mild: lesions <0.3 cm, asymptomatic
Moderate: 0.3–0.5 cm, intermittent pelvic pain or spotting
Severe: >0.5 cm, persistent pain, heavy menstrual bleeding, or haemoperitoneum
sections.p: Severity is graded by size and symptom burden rather than a formal staging system.

b: Portal hypertension (most common in low‑resource settings with schistosomiasis or hepatitis B)
Pelvic congestion syndrome (multiple ovarian/uterine veins)
Pregnancy‑related venous engorgement
Obstructive lesions (fibroids, ovarian masses)
Thrombophilia or sickle‑cell disease causing venous stasis
sections.p: Varices develop when venous pressure in the pelvis rises or when local venous drainage is obstructed.

b: Bluish‑red nodules on laparoscopy
Tenderness on deep pelvic examination
Occasional haemoperitoneum after trauma or surgery
sections.p: Patients may be asymptomatic or report vague pelvic discomfort, dysmenorrhoea, or abnormal uterine bleeding.
When imaging is unavailable, rely on clinical signs of portal hypertension and intra‑operative visualisation.

t.b: Does the lesion have venous flow characteristics? – Confirms varix if low‑resistance, compressible flow is seen.
Maps extent of venous dilatation and rules out masses – Shows enhancing tubular structures in the broad ligament.
Direct visual confirmation – Identifies typical 0.2–0.4 cm bluish‑red lesions.

t.a: Serum portal pressure surrogate (e.g., platelet count, splenomegaly on exam)
t.b: Is portal hypertension likely? – Low platelets <150 000/µL or palpable spleen suggest underlying portal hypertension.

b: Acute haemoperitoneum from rupture
Persistent pelvic pain impairing quality of life
Bleeding that worsens anaemia
sections.p: Complications are rare but can be serious.

b: Portal hypertension: beta‑blockers (e.g., propranolol) to lower portal pressure; consider endoscopic variceal ligation if oesophageal varices present.
Pelvic congestion: hormonal suppression (combined oral contraceptives) to reduce venous flow; consider embolisation of ovarian veins if available.
Surgical excision or ligation of the varix during laparotomy if bleeding or severe pain persists.
Supportive care: iron supplementation for anaemia, analgesics (paracetamol) for pain.
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then address the varices.

b: Repeat Doppler ultrasound every 6–12 months if symptomatic
Screen for liver disease (ultrasound, LFTs) in patients with varices
Educate patients on avoiding prolonged standing and heavy lifting
sections.p: Monitor for recurrence and for progression of underlying portal hypertension.

b: Endometriotic implants – both appear as bluish lesions but endometriosis is brown‑black, often adherent, and associated with cyclical pain.
Pelvic lymphangioma – cystic, translucent lesions rather than solid bluish nodules.
Normal Doppler flow does not exclude small varices; visual inspection remains key.
Low platelet count may be due to malaria or HIV, not only portal hypertension.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden severe lower abdominal pain with signs of shock (possible rupture)
Rapid drop in haemoglobin or overt vaginal bleeding
New onset of high‑grade fever suggesting secondary infection
